outcome: No accepted resolution or refutation has appeared since 26 January 2024. The gap-6-specific claims are self-published Zenodo preprints (Zhang, Zhang and Zhang, June to August 2026; Lynch, January 2026) with no engagement found, and the 2026 bounded-gap wave (H1 bounds of 240, 236, 212, 186 and 182) concerns the smallest gap that recurs infinitely often, not the gap 6 itself.
problem_asks: One yes/no question: are there infinitely many sexy primes? Per Wikipedia's definition, a sexy prime is a prime that differs from another prime by 6, so the question is whether there are infinitely many primes p with p and p+6 both prime (equivalently, infinitely many pairs (p, p+6) of primes; p-6 is the same pair read backwards). The statement asks for nothing else: no bound, density, asymptotic count or gap-size claim is requested. A proof that the set is infinite settles it; finitely many pairs, a density statement, or a bound on some other gap does not.

events.what_happened: D. H. J. Polymath, 'Variants of the Selberg sieve, and bounded intervals containing many primes', arXiv:1407.4897 (first submitted 18 July 2014; v4 22 December 2014); published in Research in the Mathematical Sciences in 2014 (DOI 10.1186/s40687-014-0012-7, as cited on the Axiom project page). Establishes unconditionally that the liminf of prime gaps H1 is at most 246. Conditionally on the generalized Elliott-Halberstam conjecture, establishes H1 at most 6, in the form: for any admissible triple, infinitely many n have at least two of n+h1, n+h2, n+h3 prime. The abstract also says that, via Selberg's parity problem, purely sieve methods cannot give more than this.
events.revisions: v1 18 Jul 2014; v4 22 Dec 2014 (arXiv listing). Journal version 2014 (DOI above; journal page not opened).
events.delivers: Unconditionally: some gap of at most 246 between consecutive primes recurs infinitely often (H1 at most 246). Conditionally on the generalized Elliott-Halberstam conjecture: H1 at most 6. The unconditional result says nothing about gap 6 specifically; the conditional result gives infinitely many gaps of size at most 6 (not specifically 6) under an unproven hypothesis. The arXiv abstract does not mention sexy primes or the pair (0,6). Wikipedia's claim that the sexy prime conjecture is equivalent to the generalized Elliott-Halberstam conjecture is not established by this abstract, and I did not verify it in the full text.
events.remains: Unconditionally, whether the pattern p, p+6 recurs infinitely often; the conditional result is not a proof of the unconditional statement.

checked_by.where: https://doi.org/10.1186/s40687-014-0012-7 (cited on the Axiom project page; not opened)

events.direction: Neither proves nor refutes the sexy question. Its conditional H1 at most 6 is the closest the literature comes to gap 6, and it is conditional.

events.what_happened: James Maynard, 'Small gaps between primes', arXiv:1311.4600 (November 2013; Annals of Mathematics 181 (2015), DOI 10.4007/annals.2015.181.1.7 as cited on the Axiom project page). Establishes H1 at most 600 unconditionally and that H_m is finite for every m. Under the Elliott-Halberstam conjecture, H1 at most 12 (per a search snippet of Wikipedia's bounded-gaps material). Tao obtained a similar result independently.
events.delivers: Unconditional H1 at most 600; H_m finite for all m; conditional H1 at most 12. Nothing about the pattern (0,6) specifically.
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks, including whether gap 6 recurs infinitely often.
events.direction: Neighbouring bounded-gap result; no bearing on the sexy question's answer.

events.revisions: Published in the Annals of Mathematics (2014) per the Annals search result; not opened.

events.what_happened: Ashish Mor and Surbhi Gupta, 'On Existence of Prime K-Tuples Conjecture for Positive Proportion of Admissible K-Tuples', Baghdad Science Journal vol. 21 issue 3 (2024), pp. 1073-1079. Claims that the prime k-tuples conjecture holds for a positive proportion of admissible k-tuples, unconditionally, refining the methods of Goldston-Pintz-Yildirim and Maynard.
events.revisions: None found. Journal publication date and DOI differ between the landing page (10.21123/bsj.2023.8635) and the PDF header (10.21123/bsj.2023.5368), per a search summary.
events.delivers: Claims a positive-proportion result over all admissible k-tuples. It does not single out the admissible pair {0,6}, so a positive proportion of tuples would cover the sexy pattern only if that pattern happens to be among the typical tuples, which the abstract does not say.
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks, and in particular the specific admissible pair {0,6}.

checked_by.qualification: A journal publication; the review process was not examined

events.doubts: A search summary reports that the abstract's central claim closely mirrors Maynard's 2015 theorem (positive proportion of admissible k-tuples), with no clear statement of what is new. I could not verify this because the journal's own page failed to load (DNS error), so the date and claim come from a search snippet of the PDF. No expert or citing work was found.
events.direction: A statement about admissible k-tuples in general, with no claim about {0,6}. Does not bear directly on the sexy question's answer.

events.what_happened: Fred B. Holt, 'Eratosthenes sieve supports the k-tuple conjecture', arXiv:2502.20470 (v1 27 February 2025; v2 29 April 2025; v3 8 July 2025). Models the Eratosthenes sieve as a discrete dynamic system. Per the abstract, shows that every admissible instance of every admissible constellation of gaps arises and persists in the sieve, and that the population counts are consistent with the Hardy-Littlewood (1923) estimates. The statement of Theorem 1.1 (a finite-stage statement for stages up to p_k) comes from a search snippet, not from my reading of the full paper.
events.revisions: v1 27 Feb 2025; v2 29 Apr 2025; v3 8 Jul 2025 (arXiv abstract page).
events.delivers: A statement about admissible instances occurring at each finite sieve stage, plus heuristic agreement with Hardy-Littlewood. It establishes no infinitude of any admissible pattern, and the abstract does not mention the pair {0,6}.
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks. The k-tuple conjecture for the admissible pair {0,6} is exactly the sexy question, and this paper does not deliver it.
events.doubts: The title says 'supports', not 'proves'; the Hardy-Littlewood comparison is described as 'consistent with' an estimate, which is heuristic. A later Holt preprint (arXiv:2603.25896, search snippet only, not opened) cites this work as its basis.
events.direction: Does not answer the sexy question in either direction; a finite-stage structural result in the k-tuple area.

events.what_happened: Brendan Lynch, 'Unconditional Analytical Closure of Polignac's Conjecture via UFT-F Spectral Invariance', Zenodo record 18369489 (v1, 25 January 2026; self-published, CC BY 4.0). The record claims that 'non-vanishing spectral density \hat{P}(h) > 0 is a structural requirement for stability at every even gap h', and presents this as an unconditional analytical proof of Polignac's conjecture (infinitely many prime pairs with difference h, for every even h). Supporting material: GPU computation of prime-pair correlation sums up to N = 10^9 for tested gaps (h = 2, 4, 6, 30 per the record's own wording), and a log-log regression slope described as consistent with an error term under RH.
events.revisions: Only v1 listed on the record page; the Versions section is empty in the captured text.
events.delivers: As written: a claimed general Polignac statement, which if correct would include the even gap 6 and so the sexy pattern. What the record actually supplies for gap 6 is numerical evidence up to N = 10^9 and an error-term claim that is explicitly conditional on RH (the abstract: 'under RH (β ≤ 1/2)'). No unconditional result for gap 6 is delivered.
events.remains: Per the record's own content, the infinitude of gap-6 pairs is asserted rather than shown unconditionally, and the record's RH dependence is not removed.
events.doubts: (1) The title says 'Unconditional' but the error-term claim is conditional on RH in the record's own abstract. (2) Support is numerical, for finitely many gaps up to 10^9, which cannot establish infinitude. (3) A companion record by the same author (search snippet, not opened) describes the central 'Anti-Collision Identity' as a conjectured L1-integrability condition, which would mean the argument rests on an unproven input. (4) The same author has other self-published claims (search snippets: the seven Clay problems, Montgomery's conjecture; not opened). (5) No peer review, Lean formalisation or expert engagement found.
events.direction: If correct, cuts toward yes (infinitely many sexy primes). As written, the claim rests on numerics and an RH-conditional error term, so it does not deliver a proof for gap 6.

events.what_happened: Yue Zhang (listed role: annotator), Xiang Zhang and Fadong Zhang (listed role: data manager), no affiliations shown, Zenodo record 20758563, initially titled 'A Proof of Polignac's Conjecture via Translational Tower Sieve and Precise Cutting' (v11, 19 June 2026). The latest version seen (v15, 25 August 2026) is retitled 'Fixed-Window Tower Sieve with Precision Period Cutting: A Proof of Polignac's Conjecture'. The stated conjecture is 'for every positive integer k, there exist infinitely many prime pairs (p, p+2k)', and the main claim is: 'In this paper, we present a rigorous proof of this conjecture within the fixed-window tower sieve framework.' With k = 3 this is the sexy statement. The method is described as elementary (CRT counting lemma, Chebyshev, Mertens), a three-layer periodic cutting strategy and a recurrence whose iteration gives unbounded survivor counts.
events.revisions: v11 19 Jun 2026 (record page, fetched); v12 24 Jun 2026 (search snippet); v15 25 Aug 2026 (latest-version page, fetched; retitled and argument changed according to the search summary). Versions v1 to v10 were not seen, so the first upload date is unknown and may be earlier than 19 June 2026.
events.delivers: Claims the full statement for every k, including k = 3 (infinitely many primes p with p+6 prime). No restriction is stated. If the argument were correct it would settle this bullet. As of my reading it is an assertion with no verification.
events.remains: Nothing, if the claim held; no verification found.
events.doubts: (1) Self-published Zenodo deposit; no affiliations; authors listed with roles 'Annotator' and 'Data manager'. (2) The record says the argument 'successfully bypasses the parity barrier of classical sieve methods' but, in what I could read, does not explain how. The Polymath8b paper (arXiv:1407.4897, opened) says that, via Selberg's parity problem, purely sieve methods cannot give more than H1 at most 6 under the generalized Elliott-Halberstam conjecture, so a claim to pass the parity barrier needs a mechanism the 2014 paper treats as a limit of sieve methods. (3) The record changed title and argument between v11 and v15 (search summary and fetched pages). (4) The same author group's record of 6 June 2026 claims an elementary proof of the twin prime conjecture 'bypassing the parity obstacle' (separate event below). (5) No Lean formalisation, reviewer or expert engagement found; the record itself mentions none.
events.direction: If correct, cuts toward yes (infinitely many sexy primes). It is a claimed unconditional proof, not conditional, but I found no verification of it.

events.what_happened: Yue Zhang (listed as contact person), Xiang Zhang and Fadong Zhang (data managers), Zenodo record 20565919, 'Translational Tower Sieve and Precise Period Cutting: An Elementary Proof of the Twin Prime Conjecture and Bypassing the Parity Obstacle' (dated 6 June 2026; v12 seen, a newer version exists). Main claim: 'Applying Mertens' theorem gives N_t to infinity, thus proving the Twin Prime Conjecture.'
events.revisions: Dated 6 Jun 2026; v12 seen; later versions exist but were not read.
events.delivers: Claims infinitely many pairs differing by 2 (twin primes). It does not mention sexy primes or Polignac's conjecture. Neighbouring question; it does not address gap 6.
events.doubts: Same author group and method family as the Polignac record above; claims to bypass the parity obstacle without a visible mechanism; self-published; no reviewer or expert engagement found. Elementary proof claims of the twin prime conjecture have been wrong before, which a search summary notes (AoPS wiki entry; not opened).
events.direction: Neighbouring (gap 2). Claims yes for the twin-prime question; no bearing on gap 6 except as a signal about the author group.

events.what_happened: Alexander Caicedo and Julio C. Ramos-Fernandez, 'Structural Existence of Prime Constellations: Asymptotic Spectral Stability in Finite Sieve Windows', arXiv:2512.03288 (v1, 2 December 2025; subjects math.NT, math.CO, math.SP). The abstract argues, via a 'Variance Gap' (variance growing linearly with the mean rather than quadratically) and a 'Null Hypothesis' framing, that the existence of prime constellations is 'a mandatory consequence of the system's finite spectral bandwidth'. The only example in the abstract is twin primes. A search summary says the paper has a section on sexy primes with a doubled local density at 3 (C6 = 2C2), but I could not confirm this: the PDF body was unreadable and the abstract never mentions p+6.
events.delivers: As read: a general claim that prime constellations exist, with no theorem stated for p+6 in the abstract. Per the unverified search summary, any sexy section concerns a local density or constant ratio, not infinitude.
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks, unless the full text contains a proof for p+6 that I could not read.
events.doubts: The 'Null Hypothesis' and 'Variance Gap' framing are not standard in the sieve literature; the abstract names the Parity Barrier as the obstacle to classical sieves and does not show visibly how it is passed. Single version; no reviewer or expert engagement found.
events.direction: As read, a heuristic or structural argument for the existence of constellations including, if the sexy section exists, p+6. Not established as a proof.

The abstract claims to prove that each Collatz sequence returns to 1. Early search snippets reported a section titled 'Theorem of sexy primes' (a numbered sexy-primes theorem derived from a lemma about even gaps; Lemma 21.2 mentioned in one summary). A later search did not reproduce that section, and the PDF body was unreadable to my fetch tool. Whether the sexy-prime claim is in the paper, and in which version, is therefore not established.

events.delivers: If the snippet is right, a claimed proof that there are infinitely many sexy primes, inside a Collatz argument. Unverified; the abstract itself does not mention sexy primes.
events.remains: If the claim stands, nothing. The paper's main claim (the Collatz problem) is itself regarded as open.
events.doubts: A search summary of a snippet described the sexy argument as 'structured as "if the statement holds, the lemma is true; otherwise..."' with the excerpt not completing the reasoning. I could not confirm this. The abstract's Collatz claim is not accepted by any source I found. No expert engagement found.
events.direction: If the sexy section exists as described, cuts toward yes. Not verified.

events.what_happened: OpenAI preprint 'Improved Short Gaps Between Primes' (PDF on cdn.openai.com, which I could not read), dated 30 August 2026 and announced 3 September 2026 (per the Breakthrough Tracker record). Claims the liminf of consecutive prime gaps is at most 186, presented as an improvement on 246 and a concurrent 240. The tracker says the proof is attributed to GPT-6 Astra. The companion repository github.com/openai/PrimeGaps186 (opened README) contains a Lean 4 development deriving DHL[40,2] and then the bound 186, with a Python-FLINT numerical certificate. The README says the result is conditional on three named axioms: PrimeGap186.kloosterman3_bound (Kl3 Kloosterman bound, attributed to Deligne's theorem as presented in Katz's book); PrimeGap186.kloosterman2_correlation_bound (K2 correlation bound, attributed to Fouvry, Kowalski and Michel); and PrimeGap186.physical_integral_bounds (104 outer and 45 inner physical-integral upper bounds plus three cap bounds, numerical inputs). The README says these 'remain unproved' in Lean.
events.revisions: None found. The tracker record was last checked 7 September 2026.
events.delivers: H1 at most 186, conditional on the three axioms listed above (not Lean-proved). Neighbouring question: a bound that some gap of at most 186 recurs infinitely often; it does not show that gap 6 does.
events.directly_checkable: The Python certificate prime_gap_186_certificate.py checks the numerical inputs; per the tracker, 'the numerical certificate does not discharge those axioms'.
events.doubts: (1) Conditional on three inputs, two of which are cited estimates and one numerical; the README says the build 'passed without errors or warnings' and that Challenge.lean has 'three intentional theorem placeholders', without saying whether these are sorry. (2) The tracker says 'no independent human semantic review was located'. (3) Commentators disagree about whether the conditional status is understated (search summaries of social-media comments; not opened). (4) The OpenAI PDF itself was unreadable to me, so the AI attribution rests on the tracker's rendering of it.
events.direction: Claims H1 at most 186 (conditionally), beating 246 on the smallest-gap question. Does not move the gap-6 question.

disputes.summary: A search summary reports that the Mor and Gupta (2024) abstract's central claim, a positive proportion of admissible k-tuples satisfying the prime k-tuples conjecture, closely mirrors Maynard's 2015 Annals theorem. Not verified because the journal page failed to load.

The 212 bound is credited to human authors (Charton et al.), with the analytic ideas attributed by the authors to Stadlmann's work, and to AxiomProver for formal verification. The 186 bound is credited by OpenAI to GPT-6 Astra. The 182 manuscript is credited to GPT-6 Astra on a UCLA faculty listing. None of these is a sexy-prime claim.

Sources disagree on the Song and Yue date (search summary: 2 September 2026; ePrint page: received 4 September, approved 9 September) and on whether the Axiom 246 formalisation assumes Bombieri-Vinogradov (search snippet: yes; fetched project page: not mentioned).

summary: Found nothing that settles the question. The record holds three kinds of material. (1) The gap-6 question itself has several claimed proofs, all self-published on Zenodo or arXiv, none reviewed, none formalised, none engaged with publicly: the Zhang, Zhang and Zhang records (6 June 2026 twin-prime claim; 19 June to 25 August 2026 Polignac claim whose stated conjecture includes k = 3, i.e. p and p+6), the Lynch record (25 January 2026, Polignac for every even gap, supported by numerics up to 10^9 and an RH-conditional error term), the Caicedo and Ramos-Fernandez arXiv preprint (2 December 2025, a general constellation claim whose sexy section I could not confirm), and an older Tan Collatz preprint (2011) whose 'Theorem of sexy primes' appeared only in search snippets I could not confirm in the text. Of these, the Zhang, Zhang and Zhang claim is the one that directly states this bullet's question. Its parity-barrier claim runs against the Polymath8b statement that sieve methods cannot give more than H1 at most 6 under the generalized Elliott-Halberstam conjecture. (2) The best published work on gap 6 is conditional: Polymath8b (2014) gives H1 at most 6 under the generalized Elliott-Halberstam conjecture, and the unconditional bound is 246. (3) The 2026 bounded-gap wave is large and substantially AI-attributed: Stadlmann (240, human), Song and Yue (236, human), Charton et al. with Axiom (212, human authors with AxiomProver credited for formal verification), OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra (186, conditional on three named inputs, Lean development at the repository), and Sharifi's manuscript credited to GPT-6 Astra (182, PDF unread). These move H1, the smallest gap that recurs infinitely often. They do not show that gap 6 recurs, and I have recorded them as neighbouring events. The OpenAI openai/math release of 6 October 2026 (719 to 722 manuscripts) has no title on sexy primes, Polignac, Dickson or k-tuples in the full CONTENTS listing I read, so it does not appear as an event. Close calls: (a) whether a Polignac proof counts for this bullet, since section 2.1 says stronger forms settle nothing here but a proof of a stronger statement logically covers it; I have recorded the Polignac claims as bearing on this bullet and left the weighing to the later pass; (b) whether a bounded-gap result is an analogue (I recorded it as a different question); (c) the Wikipedia claim that the sexy prime conjecture is equivalent to gaps of size at most 6 recurring infinitely often, which I did not verify (gaps of 2 or 4 could recur without any pair (p, p+6)). For AI, the only system in ai.systems is GPT-6 Astra in two neighbouring H1 events, both resting on secondary or unreadable primary sources for the 186 result; no AI system is named on any gap-6-specific event.
competing_reading: A reader could treat the Zhang, Zhang and Zhang Polignac record (June to August 2026) as a live, if unverified, claimed resolution, because it states the bullet's question and includes k = 3 explicitly; on that reading the problem's status depends on whether that claim survives review, and the record is a candidate for expert checking. Against this, the claim is self-published, its method is said to bypass a barrier that Polymath8b presents as a limit of sieve methods, and nothing in the sources engages with it. A second reading treats the 2026 bounded-gap wave as relevant progress on this bullet, on the grounds that a smaller H1 is a step towards the sexy question; the scope rule (section 2.1) and the statement's specific pattern (0,6) make that reading hard to sustain, since H1 at most 186 says only that some gap of at most 186 recurs. A third reading counts the 2014 conditional result as partial progress, because Wikipedia describes the sexy conjecture as equivalent to a generalized Elliott-Halberstam statement; the abstract I read does not say that, and I did not verify it.
what_would_settle_it: For the Zhang, Zhang and Zhang Polignac record: a referee report or expert write-up identifying whether the recurrence and the parity-barrier step hold, or a formal (Lean) proof of the key step. For the Lynch record: an unconditional argument without numerics or RH. For the Tan 2011 preprint: the full PDF text, to see whether a sexy-prime theorem exists and in which version. For the H1 wave: independent review of the 186 and 212 arguments and of the three OpenAI inputs, and the Lean status of the 186 repository. For the bullet itself, nothing short of an accepted proof (or a proof of Polignac's conjecture, which implies it) would change the status; a conditional result would not.
